Stereo output for 3D panels

Source: R/stereo-3d.R
stereo_3d.Rd

stereo_3d() configures coord_3d() to draw every panel for two eyes, as a side-by-side stereo pair or as one anaglyph to view through coloured glasses, in the manner of the stereo displays of tourr (display_stereo(), anaglyph()) and ggthreed (stat_anaglyph()).

Usage

stereo_3d(
  mode = c("pair", "cross", "anaglyph"),
  separation = 3,
  colours = c("red", "cyan")
)

Arguments

mode

"pair", "cross" or "anaglyph".

separation

Angle between the two eye directions in degrees, greater than 0 and less than 90.

colours

Two filter colours, the left eye's first, as in the colour glasses used to view an anaglyph.

Value

A stereo configuration for the stereo argument of coord_3d().

Details

The two eye cameras turn about the camera target by half of separation each way, about the vertical axis of the image. For a level camera without roll this is an azimuth offset of separation / 2 per eye. Both eyes look at the target, so the target lies in the page plane: geometry in front of it appears in front of the page, geometry behind it behind the page. In an orthographic view the two images differ only horizontally. Both eyes share one magnification and one axis-label reserve, so the images have the same scale.

"pair" places the left-eye image on the left, for parallel (wall-eyed) free viewing and stereoscopes; "cross" places it on the right, for cross-eyed viewing. Each panel then holds the two images side by side and is twice as wide as high.

"anaglyph" draws both images into one panel. Each image is reduced to its luminance and seen through its filter colour: the panel is the product of the left image tinted toward the complement of the left filter and the right image tinted toward the complement of the right filter, so with red and cyan filters the red channel holds the left image and the green and blue channels the right image. Paint seen identically by both eyes, such as the panel background, keeps its grey level. Colour and fill scales then carry only luminance; coord_3d() warns when the plot has one. With the vector and hybrid backends the two images are drawn as monochrome passes composited with a multiply blend (grid group compositing, R 4.2 or later) when the graphics device supports it, such as the ragg, Cairo, svg and pdf devices. Otherwise, and always with the raster backend, both images are rendered offscreen at the backend's dpi with ragg and composited per colour channel into one image; on a white background this matches the blended result.

view_3d() shows the plot from the central camera, without stereo.

See also

coord_3d(), facet_views(), whose views each become a stereo pair.

Examples

d <- expand.grid(x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 25), y = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 25))
d$z <- exp(-3 * (d$x^2 + d$y^2))
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(d, ggplot2::aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85", colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2)
p + coord_3d(stereo = stereo_3d("pair"))
p + coord_3d(stereo = stereo_3d("cross", separation = 5))
p + coord_3d(stereo = stereo_3d("anaglyph", colours = c("red", "cyan")))
